newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate opens debate on gay job bias bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate opens debate on gay job bias bill.

text.p: Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy argued on Friday for a bill protecting Americans from being fired for being homosexual but Republican Sen. Orrin Hatch said some employers had "honest moral objections" to gays and lesbians.

The exchange took place during the Senate's first-ever debate on extending workplace rights to gays and lesbians, embodied in a bill offered by Kennedy, who said the measure was the latest battle in a war against discrimination.

The Massachusetts Democrat cited laws that ended slavery, Japanese internment camps and discrimination against women, racial and religious minorities and the disabled. "Each bill is an acknowledgment that America can rise above its prejudices," he said.

His bill would add sexual orientation to the list of attributes that cannot be used as a reason for firing people or refusing to hire them. Kennedy and others cited the case of a woman who had lost her job, with the reason given that she violated company policy by being a lesbian.

But Hatch, the Senate Judiciary Committee chairman, said "many employers have honest moral, religious-based objections to hiring homosexuals." The Utah Reublican said a single male teacher holding hands with another male outside a school would be wrong "in terms of role models for school children and the other concerns parents and educators might have."

But Kennedy took issue with Hatch. "We went through a period not long ago when a lot of people had moral beliefs, ethical beliefs, not to associate with blacks, Latinos, Asian-Americans," Kennedy said. But civil rights laws say "individuals cannot use those beliefs in order to discriminate against fellow Americans," he said.

The job descrimination bill had originally been designed to be offered as an amendment to the Defence of Marriage bill, which was to have been considered on Thursday. But after senators objected, a compromise was struck whereby the bills will be voted on as separate measures on Tuesday.

The Defence of Marriage bill has already passed the House of Representatives. It would prohibit federal Social Security and veterans benefits for spouses in same-sex marriages, should they become legal in any state. It also says no state need recognise same-sex marriages in other states.
A court case now making its way through Hawaiian courts may permit same-sex marriages there in several years. Passage of the bill is expected and President Bill Clinton has said he would sign it.
